summary.text: Lesson 1-5 of enVision Math Grade 4, the topic's math-practices lesson: constructing arguments about place value and comparison. Covers conjectures, what a complete argument contains, counterexamples, judging someone else's reasoning, and translating number names correctly.

why.text: This is the lesson where the answer stops being enough — the argument IS the assignment. That is how her tests will grade explanation questions all year, and honestly, it is the most transferable skill in the whole topic.

objectives.text: State what a conjecture is and test one with numbers
Construct a complete comparison argument that names the deciding place
Break an always-claim with a single counterexample
Judge another student's reasoning, including right-answer-wrong-method

parentNote.text: Built from the HW 1-5 sheet, which is the practices lesson closing Topic 1. The recurring move: judge REASONING separately from ANSWERS — two questions feature arguments that reach correct conclusions through broken methods, because that distinction is exactly what her sheet's Critique Reasoning problems test. The ten-times conjecture questions echo the sheet's planet-equator task with fresh scenarios.

nextUp.text: Quiz in one sitting. On every question, ask what the ARGUMENT is, not just the answer.

cards.def:
**A statement believed to be true that has not been proven yet.**
• "Arizona had more retail sales than Massachusetts" is a conjecture until the numbers back it.
• Testing conjectures is the whole job of this lesson.

**Clear and complete reasoning, correct numbers and symbols, and something that justifies each step.**
• Drawings, place-value blocks and number lines all count as justification.
• "Because it looks bigger" is a feeling, not an argument.

**One example that breaks a claim.**
• The claim "any number with more 9s is greater" dies against 999 < 1,000.
• One counterexample defeats an always-statement completely — no second one needed.
cards.hint: To attack a claim, hunt for the single case that breaks it.

cards.def:
**An argument about comparing must march places from the left — quoting two stray digits proves nothing.**
• $13,637 > $13,533 because the HUNDREDS differ: 600 > 500.
• Saying "7 > 3" compares the ones — those digits never got a vote.

**Translate number names carefully: three hundred thousand, twenty-seven is 300,027 — not 327,000.**
• Missing places fill with zeros.
• Most wrong arguments about big numbers start with a wrong translation.
cards.hint: Write the places as blanks first: ___ ___ ___, ___ ___ ___. Then fill what the words actually say.

opts: A statement believed true but not yet proven
A statement that has been proven
A number written in expanded form
A kind of rounding
questions.hint: It is a claim waiting for an argument.
steps: A conjecture is a belief about how something works.
It might be right or wrong — nobody has shown which yet.
Your job is to build the argument that settles it.

ex.main: **A statement believed true but not proven.** Once a solid argument lands, it stops being a conjecture.
ex.tip: Scientists and mathematicians both live on conjectures. The argument is what separates believing from knowing.

questions.q: Which of these is a real math argument that 5,280 > 5,190?
opts: The thousands match, and in the hundreds 2 > 1, so 5,280 is greater
5,280 looks bigger
80 is bigger than 90 backwards
Both have four digits
questions.hint: A real argument names the deciding place.
steps: March from the left: thousands are 5 and 5 — equal.
Hundreds: 2 versus 1. First difference.
2 hundreds > 1 hundred, so 5,280 > 5,190. That names the place and the reason.

ex.main: **The hundreds decide: 2 > 1.** The other choices are feelings or noise — nothing a reader could check.
ex.tip: A good argument survives being checked by someone who disagrees with you.

opts: One example that shows a claim is false
An example that supports a claim
A second way of writing a number
An estimate used for checking
questions.hint: It is the single case that breaks the rule.
steps: A claim like "this always happens" promises every case works.
Finding even ONE case where it fails breaks the promise.
That one case is a counterexample, and it finishes the argument.

ex.main: **One example that shows a claim is false.** Against an always-claim, one is enough.
ex.tip: Defending a claim takes every case. Breaking one takes a single case. Attack is cheaper — use that.

questions.q: Mara claims: "$41,268 is more than $41,832 because 8 > 3." Construct the correct judgement of her argument.
opts: Her conclusion AND her method are wrong — the hundreds decide, and 2 < 8, so $41,268 is less
Her conclusion is right but her method is wrong
Her conclusion and method are both right
Her method is right but she compared the wrong numbers
questions.hint: Check the comparison honestly first, then check what her digits were.
steps: March left: 4 = 4, 1 = 1. Hundreds: 2 versus 8.
2 < 8, so $41,268 < $41,832. Her conclusion is false.
Her "8 > 3" pulled digits from different places — the ones of one number, the hundreds of the other.
So both the answer and the reasoning fail. The fix is the left-to-right march.

ex.main: **Both wrong.** Comparing digits from different places can produce any answer at all — sometimes even the right one, by luck.
ex.tip: The march exists because it never needs luck.

questions.q: A sign says a city's population is "six hundred four thousand, fifty". A student writes 604,050 and another writes 645,000. Who translated correctly?
opts: The first: six hundred four thousand is 604,—, and fifty fills in as 050
The second: the words say 645
Both are acceptable
Neither is right
questions.hint: Translate in two chunks: the thousands part, then the rest.
steps: "Six hundred four thousand" is 604 in the thousands period: 604,—.
"Fifty" is what fills the last three places: 050.
Together: 604,050.
645,000 invents a 45 the words never said — the classic mistranslation.

ex.main: **604,050.** Missing places fill with zeros; nothing in the words lets digits move houses.
ex.tip: Read number names one period at a time. The comma in the words matches the comma in the number.

questions.q: Ravi conjectures a blue whale is about ten times as long as a school bus. The whale measures 98 feet; the bus measures 40 feet. Judge the conjecture.
opts: It fails — 98 is about 100, and ten times 40 is 400, which is way past 100
It holds — both numbers are big
It holds — 98 is close to 40 × 10
It fails — whales are actually shorter than buses
questions.hint: Estimate both, then test the ten-times claim against the estimates.
steps: Estimate: the whale is about 100 feet, the bus about 40 feet.
Ten times the bus would be 40 × 10 = 400 feet.
The whale's 100 feet is nowhere near 400 — it is closer to 2 and a half times the bus.
So the conjecture fails, and the estimates are the argument.

ex.main: **It fails — ten times a bus would be 400 feet.** Testing a conjecture with rounded numbers is usually enough to settle it.
ex.tip: Estimate first. If the claim fails on estimates, exact arithmetic is not needed.

questions.q: To argue that 356,208 > 356,079, which sentence does the real work?
opts: The hundreds differ: 2 hundreds > 0 hundreds
Both numbers are in the three hundred thousands
The ones differ: 8 > 9 is false, so check again
356,208 has a 2 in it
questions.hint: The deciding sentence names the first differing place and compares it.
steps: Hundred thousands, ten thousands and thousands all match: 3, 5, 6.
The hundreds are the first difference: 2 versus 0.
2 hundreds > 0 hundreds settles it — every later digit is irrelevant.

ex.main: **The hundreds sentence.** Everything else in the list is true-but-useless, which is the difference between facts and arguments.
ex.tip: An argument is the minimum set of facts that FORCES the conclusion. Extra facts are decoration.

questions.q: Nia claims: "If you round two different numbers to the same place, the bigger number always gives the bigger rounded answer." Find the counterexample.
opts: 82 and 78 to the nearest ten: both give 80 — bigger did not give bigger
91 and 89 to the nearest ten give 90 and 90
146 and 150 give different answers
There is no counterexample; the claim is true
questions.hint: Try two different numbers that live in the same rounding neighbourhood.
steps: 82 rounds to 80 at the nearest ten. 78 also rounds to 80.
82 > 78, but the rounded answers are equal — not bigger.
The claim said "always gives the bigger", and equal is not bigger.
One counterexample, claim finished. (Both numbers just have to share a neighbourhood.)

ex.main: **82 and 78 both round to 80.** Rounding flattens differences, so "bigger stays bigger" fails whenever two numbers share a benchmark.
ex.tip: When a claim says ALWAYS, look for the flattening cases: ties, boundaries, and shared neighbourhoods.

questions.q: A newspaper claims: "Star Stadium (61,500 seats) is about ten times the size of Riverside Field (5,986 seats)." Construct the supporting argument.
opts: Round: 61,500 is about 60,000 and 5,986 is about 6,000; 6,000 × 10 = 60,000, so the claim holds
Count the digits: five beats four, so it is ten times
The claim fails because 61,500 is not exactly 59,860
61,500 − 5,986 is big, so the claim holds
questions.hint: Ten-times claims are place-value claims. Round both numbers first.
steps: Round both: 61,500 → about 60,000; 5,986 → about 6,000.
Test the claim: 6,000 × 10 = 60,000.
The estimates match the ten-times relationship almost exactly.
"About ten times" only needs the estimates to line up — exactness was never claimed.

ex.main: **Round both, then test: 6,000 × 10 = 60,000.** The word "about" means the argument runs on estimates, and that is legitimate.
ex.tip: Subtraction tells you the gap. Only the times-ten test tells you the RATIO, which is what the claim was about.

questions.q: Tomás argues: "300,027 < 316,042 because my number has a zero in the ten thousands place and hers has a one, and 0 < 1." Is his argument complete?
opts: Almost — he must first note the hundred thousands MATCH, or the comparison is not anchored
Yes — it is complete as stated
No — he should compare the ones place
No — zeros cannot be compared
questions.hint: The march has to start at the left. What did he skip?
steps: His deciding place is right: ten thousands, 0 versus 1.
But that place only decides IF every place to its left matches.
The complete argument says: hundred thousands match at 3, THEN ten thousands differ, 0 < 1.
Without the first sentence, a reader cannot know the earlier places did not already decide it.

ex.main: **Almost — the argument must first anchor the matching places.** The conclusion is right; the argument has a missing rung.
ex.tip: Complete arguments state the boring steps too. The boring steps are what make them checkable.
